newsitem.title: GERMANY: Embattled Kohl rejects reshuffle talk, euro delay.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Kohl rejects reshuffle talk, euro delay.

text.p: Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl, facing record unemployment and deadlock over sweeping tax reforms, on Sunday dismissed rumours of a cabinet reshuffle and insisted the launch of Europe's single currency would go ahead on time.

The German leader told newspaper Welt am Sonntag he was certain his "excellent" team was capable of tackling the tasks that lay ahead of them. His optimistic remarks were his last before taking off for his annual Easter fitness holiday in the Austrian alps.

Kohl said his ruling coalition was prepared to meet the opposition Social Democrats (SDP) for consensus talks on the much-needed tax reforms at any time, even before next weekend's Easter holiday, and blasted them for exploiting the deadlock to boost their standing ahead of the 1998 general election.
"We have 4.7 million unemployed and it's clear to everyone that we just don't have the time to wait for the SPD...to make up their minds," Kohl told the newspaper.
Although Kohl's coalition holds a majority of seats in the Bundestag lower house of parliament, the SPD can block most tax measures through its majority in the Bundesrat upper house.

Kohl warned SPD leaders, who pulled out of tax talks with the government in a clash over coal subsidy cuts two weeks ago, he would only resume talks without preconditions and that their blockade tactics could damage society's future chances.
"I would hope and trust that the Social Democrats would have the rational power to see these issues through," he said.

But SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said he too was ready to meet Kohl at any time, saying the government had failed to come up with acceptable proposals and that joblessness was sky-high because of huge non-wage labour costs employers had to pay.
"We don't want tax cuts for people who will put the extra cash in savings accounts, but for employers and families, who will spend it tomorrow," Lafontaine told ZDF television.
Kohl argued the 1998 tax bill, that envisages tax cuts of 30 billion marks a year, would provide a crucial boost to flagging domestic investment and the desperate job situation.
The measures are also seen as essential to help whip Germany's finances into shape for European monetary union (EMU) due to be launched on January 1, 1999.

The launch would be unthinkable without Germany, the chief motor behind EMU with France. But Germany's recent sluggish economic performance has prompted speculation that it might not be deemed economically fit enough to qualify.
Kohl brushed aside talk of delaying the Europe's planned single currency the euro, saying he was determined Germany would join in the planned launch.
"The question is not whether we are going to have European monetary union, but rather: what can we do and what must we do to ensure it starts on time," Kohl told the newspaper.

"Many self-appointed experts only want a postponement so that the project is completely put on ice. Others get cold feet when things get tough," he said, referring to many politicians and experts who say Germany may flunk the criteria.
"Postponement is out of the question," Kohl said.

Kohl said he had no plans for a cabinet reshuffle, after Stern weekly reported on Thursday Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt was under pressure from the ranks of his Free Democrat Party (FDP) to resign citing a poor performance.
Rexrodt of the FDP, junior coalition partner to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), laughed off the report and Kohl said he had no plans to swap out any members of his team.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax bill envisages cutting the main corporate and commercial income tax rates and unifying them at a rate of 40 percent. The cuts would be neutral for revenue being offset by tightening up on corporate write-offs.

The bill would also cut two points off the unpopular solidarity surcharge on income tax, raised to finance the reconstruction of eastern Germany, to 5.5 percent, lopping 7.5 billion marks off the tax burden.
The reform would be fully implemented by 1999 with income and corporate tax cuts of a total of 30 billion marks.
